title: Detecting AI-written messages
body_md:
## Read the request, not the writing style

A polished message may be written by a person, translated, edited with AI or generated from a template. A clumsy message may also be fraudulent. There is no reliable personal rule that “AI text sounds formal” or that a friendly message must contain private memories. Attackers can feed public and stolen details into a generator, while real friends can be brief, vague or stressed. The question worth answering is: **what does this message want me to do, and how can I check that request outside the message?**

Start with the action: new payment destination, gift cards, login link, one-time code, secrecy or haste. Look for a change from the person's established pattern, but use it as a reason to verify, not a conviction. If an old friend mentions your recent public job move and asks for a transfer, the job detail does not authenticate them. If a colleague uses careful AI-assisted wording to ask you to review a ticket in the existing system, that wording does not make them a fraudster.

A question about a shared memory can sometimes slow an impostor, but it is weaker than an independent callback. Answers may be online, in a compromised mailbox or guessed. Replying in the same compromised thread also lets the attacker continue the conversation. Instead open a saved contact or the service yourself. For a company invoice, compare with the supplier record and follow the payment-change process.

AI-text detectors answer a narrow statistical question under their tested conditions. NIST's published text pilot found performance varied substantially with the generator and detector; it evaluated summaries, not your friend's email. A score cannot settle authorship, much less whether the requested payment is legitimate. Do not paste private messages into an external detector just to get a number. If you cannot verify an urgent request, pause it. A real requester can be contacted through a route you choose.

**Use language as context, not identity proof.** Good grammar has never authorised a transfer. The strongest signal is the mismatch between an action with consequences and a missing independent confirmation.

widget_config.goal: Evaluate an unexpected message by its requested action and independent verification, without treating AI-writing cues as proof.
widget_config.today_action: For one trusted contact, find the saved route you would use if a message from them requested money or an account code.
widget_config.scope: General message assessment, checked 20 October 2026; NIST findings concern a specific text-summary benchmark, not universal email classification.

sources.title: NIST: 2024 GenAI text-to-text pilot
sources.scope: Published June 2025; benchmark on generated and human summaries, with detector performance varying by systems. It does not validate a detector for an individual message.

sources.title: FTC: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money
sources.scope: US consumer advice, September 2023; voice cloning, urgency, independent callback and another relative. The US reporting route is jurisdiction-specific.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: US guidance for transfer and account-change requests; secondary-channel verification and urgent bank contact after a suspected transfer. Organisational and national procedures vary.

blocks.title: Warm note from an old friend asks for money
blocks.situation: A synthetic message congratulates you on a public job change, recalls a town visible in old posts, and asks for an urgent transfer to a new account.
blocks.analysis: Personal-looking details may have public sources; elegant prose is irrelevant. Do not reply in the thread with a trivia test. Contact the friend using your existing address or number and confirm the exact request before any payment.

blocks.title: An awkward note from a real coworker
blocks.situation: Synthetic example: A colleague writes “I am reaching out regarding the matter” after using a translation tool. They ask you to read an already filed incident in your normal work system.
blocks.analysis: Formal language is not evidence of a scam or AI authorship. Open the system yourself, inspect the incident and respond through its established workflow. Avoid forwarding the private note to a detector.

blocks.title: The too-perfect invitation
blocks.setup: Synthetic scenario: a community organiser sends a polished message about an event and asks you to pay a new registration fee. You know the organiser but have not seen this fee before.

steps.prompt: What do you identify before judging the tone?

choices.text: The new fee and payment destination
choices.explanation: Payment details require verification regardless of prose style.

choices.text: Whether the opening paragraph sounds AI-written
choices.consequence: A style guess leaves the payment question open.
choices.explanation: People and generators can write in the same register.

steps.prompt: The message links to a fee page. Where do you check?

choices.text: Open the organiser’s known site or saved contact independently
choices.consequence: You compare with a source outside the message.
choices.explanation: A link supplied by the message may lead to an attacker page.

choices.text: Follow the message link because the domain looks neat
choices.consequence: You remain within the sender’s chosen path.
choices.explanation: Visual neatness does not authenticate the site.

steps.prompt: The known channel has no fee announcement and the organiser is unavailable.

choices.text: Hold payment and ask later through the known route
choices.explanation: A deadline in an unverified message is not a reason to skip the check.

choices.text: Upload the message to an AI detector and pay if its score is low
choices.consequence: Private text leaves your control and the fee stays unverified.
choices.explanation: An AI score does not decide whether the payment is authorised.

blocks.debrief: The safe decision was about the new fee, not whether the invitation used AI. A genuine organiser may still use a writing assistant. Retry steps to compare outcomes.

questions.prompt: An AI detector marks a private email “human”. Does that permit payment?

choices.text: No; verify the payment request independently
choices.explanation: Authorship classification and payment authority are different questions.

choices.text: Yes; a human score authenticates the sender
choices.explanation: Even a human-written message may be fraudulent or come from a compromised account.

questions.prompt: A genuine colleague uses a writing assistant. What does formal prose imply?

choices.text: Little about whether the request is safe
choices.explanation: Inspect the requested action in the existing workflow.

choices.text: The colleague must be an impostor
choices.explanation: Writing style is not an identity test.

questions.prompt: A sender answers a shared-history question in the suspicious thread.

choices.text: Still use an independently selected contact for a high-risk request
choices.explanation: An attacker may have researched or read the history and may control the thread.
A remembered fact is not proof of control or authorisation.
